student_passage:
The first account (0) WAS persuasive enough to make the editor believe that the story was settled. Then a second witness described the same meeting differently, to (1) ____ an extent that several apparently minor details acquired a new significance. The problem was not (2) ____ because one speaker had forgotten a date, but because the two speakers disagreed about why the meeting had taken place at all.

The editor created a table showing the points on which the accounts converged. Without this table, she would have found it hard to compare them; without the recordings, from which every entry was drawn, she would have had no way to check what each speaker had actually said. In (3) ____ of these precautions, however, a neat table could still give a misleading impression of certainty.

Agreement was by (4) ____ means proof that a detail was correct: both witnesses might have read the same later report. With (5) ____ to the disputed purpose of the meeting, neither account could be confirmed. The editor had to decide whether or (6) ____ to publish the disagreement itself. She chose to do so, making it clear that the reader would have to form a judgement of their (7) ____. The account was less tidy as a result, but more faithful to the limits of the evidence on (8) ____ it depended.
filled_passage:
The first account (0) WAS persuasive enough to make the editor believe that the story was settled. Then a second witness described the same meeting differently, to (1) such an extent that several apparently minor details acquired a new significance. The problem was not (2) only because one speaker had forgotten a date, but because the two speakers disagreed about why the meeting had taken place at all.

The editor created a table showing the points on which the accounts converged. Without this table, she would have found it hard to compare them; without the recordings, from which every entry was drawn, she would have had no way to check what each speaker had actually said. In (3) spite of these precautions, however, a neat table could still give a misleading impression of certainty.

Agreement was by (4) no means proof that a detail was correct: both witnesses might have read the same later report. With (5) regard to the disputed purpose of the meeting, neither account could be confirmed. The editor had to decide whether or (6) not to publish the disagreement itself. She chose to do so, making it clear that the reader would have to form a judgement of their (7) own. The account was less tidy as a result, but more faithful to the limits of the evidence on (8) which it depended.
